We usually index a Student-$t$ distribution by a location $\mu$, a scale $\sigma$, and degrees of freedom $\nu$. Those coordinates are convenient, but they don't really measure anything on their own. A shift of $0.5$ does very different work for a narrow distribution than for a wide one, and adding a unit of scale is not the same operation at $\sigma=1$ as it is at $\sigma=10$.

What we'd like instead is a ruler that comes from the distributions themselves, one that calls two parameter values close when their densities are hard to tell apart and far when they're easy to tell apart. The Fisher--Rao metric is exactly that ruler. For fixed $\nu$ it hands the Student-$t$ location--scale family a clean answer — a rescaled Poincaré half-plane — and most of this note lives in that case. The clean picture stops being the whole story the moment $\nu$ is allowed to move, and that is where the note ends up.

## Why geometry enters

Coordinate distance measures the wrong thing. It tells you how far apart two parameter values sit in the chart $(\mu,\sigma,\nu)$, which is not the same as how far apart the corresponding distributions are.

The Fisher information metric
$$
g_{ij}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_\theta[\partial_i\log f\,\partial_j\log f]
$$
fixes this, because it is the quadratic term in the local KL divergence:
$$
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_\theta\|p_{\theta+d\theta})
=\frac12 g_{ij}(\theta)d\theta^i d\theta^j+O(\|d\theta\|^3).
$$
Read that way, the metric records which small parameter moves are actually visible at the level of the probability laws and quietly discounts the ones that aren't. For fixed degrees of freedom it takes a pleasantly simple form — it turns out to be hyperbolic — and the next few sections work that out before I circle back to what breaks if you ignore it.

## Location–scale families

Let $g$ be a symmetric, smooth probability density on $\mathbb{R}$, and form the
location–scale family
$$
f(x;\mu,\sigma) = \frac{1}{\sigma}\,g\!\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right),
\qquad \sigma > 0.
$$

Writing $\ell = \log f$ and $z = (x-\mu)/\sigma$, one has
$\partial_\mu \ell = -\sigma^{-1} (g'/g)(z)$ and
$\partial_\sigma \ell = -\sigma^{-1}\,(1 + z\,(g'/g)(z))$.

Symmetry of $g$ kills the cross-term, so the Fisher matrix comes out diagonal:
$$
I_{\mu\mu}(\mu,\sigma) = \frac{A}{\sigma^2},\qquad
I_{\sigma\sigma}(\mu,\sigma) = \frac{B}{\sigma^2},
$$
with constants
$$
A = \int (g'/g)^2 \, g\,dz,\qquad
B = \int (1 + z\,g'/g)^2 \, g\,dz.
$$

Since $A$ and $B$ depend only on the *shape* $g$ and not on $\mu$ or $\sigma$, the
Fisher–Rao line element on the upper half-plane is
$$
\boxed{\;ds^2 = \frac{A\,d\mu^2 + B\,d\sigma^2}{\sigma^2}\;}
$$

That is a **Poincaré-type metric** for any reasonably regular symmetric location–scale family whose Fisher constants $A$ and $B$ are finite.
The Gaussian gives $A=1, B=2$; next we work out the constants for the Student-t.

## The Student-t metric

For the Student-t with $\nu$ degrees of freedom,
$$
g(z) \propto \left(1 + \tfrac{z^2}{\nu}\right)^{-(\nu+1)/2},
\qquad \frac{g'(z)}{g(z)} = -\frac{(\nu+1)\,z}{\nu + z^2}.
$$

Both integrals are standard — substitute $z = \sqrt{\nu}\,\tan\theta$ and lean on the
beta-function identities — and they give
$$
A = \frac{\nu+1}{\nu+3},\qquad
B = \frac{2\nu}{\nu+3}.
$$

So the Fisher–Rao line element is
$$
ds^2 \;=\; \frac{1}{\nu+3}\cdot\frac{(\nu+1)\,d\mu^2 + 2\nu\,d\sigma^2}{\sigma^2}.
$$

As $\nu\to\infty$ this recovers the Gaussian metric $(d\mu^2 + 2\,d\sigma^2)/\sigma^2$,
and $\nu=1$ is the Cauchy case.

## The Poincaré half-plane

Substitute $\tilde\mu = (a/b)\,\mu$ with $a=\sqrt{A}$, $b=\sqrt{B}$. Then
$$
ds^2 = b^2 \cdot \frac{d\tilde\mu^2 + d\sigma^2}{\sigma^2},
$$
which is $b^2$ times the **standard Poincaré metric** on the upper half-plane.
That metric has Gaussian curvature $-1$, and multiplying a metric by $b^2$ scales
its curvature by $1/b^2$, so
$$
\boxed{\;K_\nu = -\frac{1}{b^2} = -\frac{\nu+3}{2\nu}\;}
$$

The limiting cases:

* $\nu \to \infty$ (Gaussian): $K \to -1/2$.
* $\nu = 1$ (Cauchy): $K = -2$.
* $\nu \to 0^+$: $K \to -\infty$ — the geometry degenerates along with the tails.

## Geodesics and distance

In the rescaled coordinate $(\tilde\mu, \sigma)$ we are back to the standard
Poincaré metric, whose geodesics everyone knows:

* **vertical lines** $\tilde\mu = \text{const}$, or
* **semicircles** centred on the $\sigma=0$ axis.

Pulling these back through $\mu = (b/a)\,\tilde\mu$ stretches them horizontally by
$b/a = \sqrt{2\nu/(\nu+1)}$. In the original $(\mu,\sigma)$ coordinates, then, a
non-vertical geodesic is **half of an ellipse** centred on the line $\sigma=0$,
with horizontal semi-axis $b/a$ times the vertical one. The aspect ratio
depends only on $\nu$:

| $\nu$ | $b/a$ | shape |
|---:|---:|:---|
| $1$ (Cauchy) | $1$ | circle |
| $3$ | $\sqrt{3/2} \approx 1.22$ | slightly stretched |
| $\infty$ (Gaussian) | $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.41$ | ellipse |

## Closed-form distance

The standard Poincaré distance on $(\tilde\mu, \sigma)$ is
$d_P(P_1,P_2) = \operatorname{arccosh}(1 + \Delta)$ with
$\Delta = \tfrac{(\tilde\mu_1-\tilde\mu_2)^2 + (\sigma_1-\sigma_2)^2}{2\sigma_1\sigma_2}$.
Scaling the metric by $b^2$ scales distances by $b$, and undoing
$\tilde\mu = (a/b)\mu$ gives $(\tilde\mu_1-\tilde\mu_2)^2 = (\nu+1)/(2\nu)\cdot (\mu_1-\mu_2)^2$.
Put together,
$$
\boxed{\;
d_{\mathrm{FR}}\bigl(t_\nu(\mu_1,\sigma_1),\,t_\nu(\mu_2,\sigma_2)\bigr)
=\sqrt{\tfrac{2\nu}{\nu+3}}\;
\operatorname{arccosh}\!\left(1 + \frac{\tfrac{\nu+1}{2\nu}(\mu_1-\mu_2)^2 + (\sigma_1-\sigma_2)^2}{2\sigma_1\sigma_2}\right).
\;}
$$

In the Gaussian limit ($\nu\to\infty$) this collapses to the classical
Atkinson–Mitchell formula
$d_{\mathrm{FR}} = \sqrt{2}\,\operatorname{arccosh}(1 + (\Delta\mu^2/2 + \Delta\sigma^2)/(2\sigma_1\sigma_2))$.

```{python}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.special import gammaln

PURPLE, CORAL = "#534AB7", "#993C1D"
plt.rcParams.update({
    "figure.dpi": 110,
    "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
    "font.size": 11,
})

def metric_constants(nu):
    """Return (A, B) so that ds^2 = (A dmu^2 + B dsigma^2) / sigma^2."""
    return (nu + 1) / (nu + 3), 2 * nu / (nu + 3)

def fr_distance(mu1, s1, mu2, s2, nu):
    """Closed-form Fisher-Rao distance between two t_nu distributions."""
    f = (nu + 1) / (2 * nu)
    arg = 1 + (f * (mu1 - mu2) ** 2 + (s1 - s2) ** 2) / (2 * s1 * s2)
    b = np.sqrt(2 * nu / (nu + 3))
    return b * np.arccosh(np.maximum(1.0, arg))

def geodesic(mu1, s1, mu2, s2, nu, n=200):
    """Sample (mu, sigma) along the Fisher-Rao geodesic between two points."""
    A, B = metric_constants(nu)
    rho = np.sqrt(A / B)               # rho = a/b
    u1, u2 = rho * mu1, rho * mu2
    if abs(u1 - u2) < 1e-9:
        return np.full(n, mu1), np.linspace(s1, s2, n)
    c = ((u1 ** 2 + s1 ** 2) - (u2 ** 2 + s2 ** 2)) / (2 * (u1 - u2))
    r = np.sqrt((u1 - c) ** 2 + s1 ** 2)
    t1 = np.arctan2(s1, u1 - c)
    t2 = np.arctan2(s2, u2 - c)
    th = np.linspace(t1, t2, n)
    return (c + r * np.cos(th)) / rho, r * np.sin(th)

def t_density(x, mu, sigma, nu):
    """Properly normalised Student-t density."""
    z = (x - mu) / sigma
    logC = gammaln((nu + 1) / 2) - gammaln(nu / 2) - 0.5 * np.log(np.pi * nu) - np.log(sigma)
    logF = -((nu + 1) / 2) * np.log1p(z ** 2 / nu)
    return np.exp(logC + logF)
```

## Reading the geometry

The closed form earns its keep by telling us how to read the pictures that follow. A straight line in the chart is usually not the shortest statistical path; an equal-distance set is not a Euclidean circle; and any change in $\mu$ gets divided by $\sigma$ before it counts for anything.

### A single geodesic

Take two distributions, $P_1=t_3(-1.2,0.7)$ and $P_2=t_3(1.3,1.5)$. The shortest Fisher--Rao path between them is not the straight segment joining their coordinates — it bows upward, because travelling close to small $\sigma$ is expensive.

```{python}
#| label: fig-geodesic
#| fig-cap: "A Fisher--Rao geodesic bends away from small scale."

p1, p2, nu = (-1.2, 0.7), (1.3, 1.5), 3.0

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.2))
mu_path, s_path = geodesic(*p1, *p2, nu)
ax.plot(mu_path, s_path, color=PURPLE, lw=2, zorder=3)

# full ghost ellipse
A, B = metric_constants(nu)
rho = np.sqrt(A / B)
u1, u2 = rho * p1[0], rho * p2[0]
c = ((u1**2 + p1[1]**2) - (u2**2 + p2[1]**2)) / (2 * (u1 - u2))
r = np.sqrt((u1 - c)**2 + p1[1]**2)
th = np.linspace(0.005, np.pi - 0.005, 200)
ax.plot((c + r * np.cos(th)) / rho, r * np.sin(th),
        color=PURPLE, lw=1, ls="--", alpha=0.4, zorder=2)

ax.scatter(*p1, s=70, color=PURPLE, zorder=4, edgecolor="white", lw=1.5)
ax.scatter(*p2, s=70, color=CORAL, zorder=4, edgecolor="white", lw=1.5)
ax.annotate(f"$P_1=({p1[0]},{p1[1]})$", p1, xytext=(8, 8),
            textcoords="offset points", color=PURPLE, fontsize=10)
ax.annotate(f"$P_2=({p2[0]},{p2[1]})$", p2, xytext=(8, 8),
            textcoords="offset points", color=CORAL, fontsize=10)

d = fr_distance(*p1, *p2, nu)
ax.set_title(f"Fisher–Rao geodesic, ν = {nu}, d = {d:.3f}")
ax.set_xlabel("location μ"); ax.set_ylabel("scale σ")
ax.set_xlim(-3, 3); ax.set_ylim(0, 2.6)
ax.grid(alpha=0.3); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

### How $\nu$ changes the shape

Hold the endpoints fixed and vary $\nu$, and what changes is the horizontal stretch of the hyperbolic half-plane. Heavy Cauchy-like tails give one shape; the Gaussian limit gives another.

```{python}
#| label: fig-nu-comparison
#| fig-cap: "Changing ν changes the shape of the same endpoint-to-endpoint path."

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.2))
nus = [1.0, 3.0, 10.0, 50.0]
colors = plt.cm.viridis(np.linspace(0.15, 0.85, len(nus)))
for nu_v, col in zip(nus, colors):
    mu_p, s_p = geodesic(*p1, *p2, nu_v)
    ax.plot(mu_p, s_p, color=col, lw=2, label=f"ν = {nu_v:g}")

ax.scatter(*p1, s=70, color="black", zorder=4, edgecolor="white", lw=1.5)
ax.scatter(*p2, s=70, color="black", zorder=4, edgecolor="white", lw=1.5)
ax.set_title("Same endpoints, geodesic depends on ν")
ax.set_xlabel("location μ"); ax.set_ylabel("scale σ")
ax.set_xlim(-3, 3); ax.set_ylim(0, 2.6)
ax.legend(loc="upper right", framealpha=0.95); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

### Balls are not Euclidean balls

A Fisher--Rao ball gathers the distributions at equal information distance from the centre. Drawn in the $(\mu,\sigma)$ chart, these balls sit higher than you'd expect and curl away from $\sigma=0$. That boundary is infinitely far off, which is why a tiny Euclidean step near zero scale can amount to a large statistical move.

```{python}
#| label: fig-balls
#| fig-cap: "Fisher--Rao distance level sets from $(0,1)$ at $\\nu=3$."

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.2))
center, nu = (0.0, 1.0), 3.0
M, S = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-3, 3, 400), np.linspace(0.05, 2.6, 300))
D = fr_distance(center[0], center[1], M, S, nu)
levels = [0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0]
cs = ax.contour(M, S, D, levels=levels, colors=PURPLE, linewidths=1.2)
ax.clabel(cs, inline=True, fontsize=9, fmt="%.2f")
ax.scatter(*center, s=80, color=PURPLE, zorder=4, edgecolor="white", lw=1.5)
ax.set_title(f"Level sets of Fisher–Rao distance from (0, 1), ν = {nu}")
ax.set_xlabel("location μ"); ax.set_ylabel("scale σ")
ax.set_xlim(-3, 3); ax.set_ylim(0, 2.6); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

### Back to densities

The points in the half-plane are only a compact shorthand for densities. Here are the two distributions behind the points in the geodesic picture above.

```{python}
#| label: fig-densities
#| fig-cap: "The two densities represented by the points $P_1$ and $P_2$."

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.5))
xs = np.linspace(-5, 5, 400)
ax.fill_between(xs, t_density(xs, *p1, nu), color=PURPLE, alpha=0.2)
ax.plot(xs, t_density(xs, *p1, nu), color=PURPLE, lw=1.5,
        label=f"$t_{{{nu:g}}}({p1[0]},{p1[1]})$")
ax.fill_between(xs, t_density(xs, *p2, nu), color=CORAL, alpha=0.2)
ax.plot(xs, t_density(xs, *p2, nu), color=CORAL, lw=1.5,
        label=f"$t_{{{nu:g}}}({p2[0]},{p2[1]})$")
ax.set_xlabel("x"); ax.set_ylabel("density"); ax.legend(); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

### Curvature across degrees of freedom

```{python}
#| label: fig-curvature
#| fig-cap: "Gaussian curvature $K_\\nu = -(\\nu+3)/(2\\nu)$ of the Student-t Fisher–Rao half-plane."

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.5))
nu_grid = np.linspace(0.5, 30, 300)
K = -(nu_grid + 3) / (2 * nu_grid)
ax.plot(nu_grid, K, color=PURPLE, lw=2)
ax.axhline(-0.5, color="gray", ls=":", lw=1)
ax.axhline(-2.0, color="gray", ls=":", lw=1)
ax.text(28, -0.45, "Gaussian limit  K = −1/2", color="gray", fontsize=9, ha="right")
ax.text(28, -1.95, "Cauchy  ν = 1, K = −2", color="gray", fontsize=9, ha="right")
ax.set_xlabel("degrees of freedom ν")
ax.set_ylabel("Gaussian curvature K")
ax.set_title("Curvature of the Student-t half-plane")
ax.grid(alpha=0.3); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## Where Euclidean geometry gives wrong answers

None of this matters unless the geometry actually flips an answer somewhere, so here are a handful of cases where Euclidean distance in $(\mu,\sigma)$ ranks distributional changes the wrong way round.

To keep the comparison honest I'll also report total variation as a check at the level of probabilities:
$$
\operatorname{TV}(P,Q)=\frac12\int |p(x)-q(x)|\,dx.
$$
With equal class priors, the best possible binary classifier telling $P$ from $Q$ has accuracy
$$
\operatorname{Acc}^*(P,Q)=\frac{1+\operatorname{TV}(P,Q)}{2}.
$$
So a small TV means even the optimal classifier is barely better than guessing, and that gives the numbers in the tables below something tangible to mean.

```{python}
#| label: wrong-helpers
#| include: false
from scipy import integrate
import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import Markdown

nu0 = 3.0

def euclidean_distance(p, q):
    """Raw Euclidean distance in the displayed (mu, sigma) coordinates."""
    return float(np.linalg.norm(np.array(p[:2]) - np.array(q[:2])))

def tv_distance(p, q):
    """Numerical total variation distance between two Student-t laws."""
    val, _ = integrate.quad(
        lambda x: abs(t_density(x, *p) - t_density(x, *q)),
        -np.inf, np.inf, limit=400, epsabs=1e-8, epsrel=1e-8
    )
    return 0.5 * val

def bayes_accuracy_from_tv(tv):
    return 0.5 * (1.0 + tv)

def comparison_row(label, p, q):
    tv = tv_distance(p, q)
    return {
        "Comparison": label,
        "Euclidean": euclidean_distance(p, q),
        "Fisher–Rao": fr_distance(p[0], p[1], q[0], q[1], p[2]),
        "TV": tv,
        "Bayes accuracy": bayes_accuracy_from_tv(tv),
    }

def show_table(rows):
    """Render a Markdown table so Quarto/MathJax keeps TeX in cells."""
    df = pd.DataFrame(rows).round(4)
    headers = list(df.columns)
    lines = ["| " + " | ".join(headers) + " |",
             "| " + " | ".join(["---"] * len(headers)) + " |"]
    for _, row in df.iterrows():
        cells = []
        for h in headers:
            value = row[h]
            if isinstance(value, (float, np.floating)):
                cells.append(f"{value:.4f}")
            else:
                cells.append(str(value))
        lines.append("| " + " | ".join(cells) + " |")
    return Markdown("\n".join(lines))
```

### Same coordinate move, different statistical change

Shift the location by the same raw amount, $\Delta\mu=0.5$, once for a narrow
$t_3$ distribution and once for a wide one:

```{python}
#| label: wrong-same-euclidean-move
rows = [
    comparison_row(
        r"$t_3(0,0.2)$ vs $t_3(0.5,0.2)$",
        (0.0, 0.2, nu0), (0.5, 0.2, nu0)
    ),
    comparison_row(
        r"$t_3(0,2)$ vs $t_3(0.5,2)$",
        (0.0, 2.0, nu0), (0.5, 2.0, nu0)
    ),
]
show_table(rows)
```

By the Euclidean reckoning these are the same move. As distributions they are
nothing alike: the narrow pair is easy to separate, while the same shift barely
disturbs the wide pair. The $d\mu^2/\sigma^2$ term in the metric is precisely
this effect — a location error only means something relative to the scale it
sits on.

```{python}
#| label: fig-wrong-same-shift
#| fig-cap: "The same raw location shift is statistically large at small scale and small at large scale."

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.5))
xs = np.linspace(-2, 6, 800)
examples = [
    ((0.0, 0.2, nu0), (0.5, 0.2, nu0), "narrow"),
    ((0.0, 2.0, nu0), (0.5, 2.0, nu0), "wide"),
]
for p, q, lab in examples:
    ax.plot(xs, t_density(xs, *p), lw=1.6, label=f"{lab}: before")
    ax.plot(xs, t_density(xs, *q), lw=1.6, ls="--", label=f"{lab}: after")
ax.set_title(r"Same $\Delta\mu=0.5$, different distributional effect")
ax.set_xlabel("x"); ax.set_ylabel("density")
ax.legend(ncol=2, fontsize=9); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

### A ranking reversal

A starker failure. Pair A moves only $0.1$ in raw location; pair B moves a full
$5$. By Euclidean distance B wins easily. But A is extremely narrow and B is very
wide, so once you look at the distributions the verdict flips.

```{python}
#| label: wrong-ranking-reversal
rows = [
    comparison_row(
        r"A: $t_3(0,0.05)$ vs $t_3(0.1,0.05)$",
        (0.0, 0.05, nu0), (0.1, 0.05, nu0)
    ),
    comparison_row(
        r"B: $t_3(0,10)$ vs $t_3(5,10)$",
        (0.0, 10.0, nu0), (5.0, 10.0, nu0)
    ),
]
show_table(rows)
```

Euclidean distance is answering the coordinate question correctly and the
statistical question wrongly: it ranks the raw $5$-unit move as the larger one,
whereas Fisher--Rao distance, TV distance, and optimal classification accuracy
all agree that the tiny $0.1$ move at small scale is the bigger change in
distribution.

### Scale changes are multiplicative

Euclidean geometry misreads scale too. In Fisher--Rao geometry, stretching
$\sigma$ to $2\sigma$ costs the same information distance wherever you start,
since along a vertical geodesic
$$
d_{\mathrm{FR}}\bigl(t_\nu(\mu,\sigma),t_\nu(\mu,c\sigma)\bigr)
= \sqrt{\frac{2\nu}{\nu+3}}\,|\log c|.
$$
At $\nu=3$ the prefactor is one, so the distance is just $|\log c|$.

```{python}
#| label: wrong-scale-multiplicative
rows = [
    comparison_row(
        r"doubling: $t_3(0,1)$ vs $t_3(0,2)$",
        (0.0, 1.0, nu0), (0.0, 2.0, nu0)
    ),
    comparison_row(
        r"doubling: $t_3(0,10)$ vs $t_3(0,20)$",
        (0.0, 10.0, nu0), (0.0, 20.0, nu0)
    ),
    comparison_row(
        r"add one: $t_3(0,10)$ vs $t_3(0,11)$",
        (0.0, 10.0, nu0), (0.0, 11.0, nu0)
    ),
]
show_table(rows)
```

Euclidean geometry puts the two doublings at distances $1$ and $10$; the
statistical geometry calls them the very same change. Going the other way,
adding one unit of scale at $\sigma=10$ is almost invisible next to doubling from
$1$ to $2$, even though both have a raw scale increment of $1$.

### Wrong nearest neighbor

For a last example, take a query distribution
$$
Q=t_3(0,1)
$$
and two candidate prototypes
$$
A=t_3(0.2,0.05),\qquad B=t_3(0.1,2).
$$
Which one is closer to $Q$?

```{python}
#| label: wrong-nearest-neighbour
Q = (0.0, 1.0, nu0)
A = (0.2, 0.05, nu0)
B = (0.1, 2.0, nu0)
rows = [
    comparison_row(r"$Q$ vs $A=t_3(0.2,0.05)$", Q, A),
    comparison_row(r"$Q$ vs $B=t_3(0.1,2)$", Q, B),
]
show_table(rows)
```

A nearest-neighbour rule on Euclidean distance picks $A$, since $(0.2,0.05)$ is
marginally closer to $(0,1)$ in raw coordinates than $(0.1,2)$ is. As
distributions, though, $A$ is the far one — a narrow spike — while $B$ is just a
moderate change of scale. Fisher--Rao, TV, and Bayes accuracy all prefer $B$.

That, more than the tidy formula, is why one bothers with the Poincaré metric.
It keeps nearest-neighbour search, clustering, interpolation, and model
comparison from mistaking proximity in coordinates for proximity in
distribution.


## Checks for the fixed-$\nu$ formulas

Before promoting $\nu$ to a coordinate, it's worth checking the fixed-slice formulas against direct numerical integration — mostly to catch the sign and scaling slips that are easy to make here.

```{python}
#| label: verify-fixed
from scipy import integrate
from IPython.display import HTML, display


def g_std(z, nu):
    logC = gammaln((nu+1)/2) - gammaln(nu/2) - 0.5*np.log(np.pi*nu)
    return np.exp(logC - ((nu+1)/2)*np.log1p(z**2/nu))


def dz_logg(z, nu):           # (g'/g)(z)
    return -(nu+1)*z/(nu+z**2)


# (a) Fisher constants A, B by direct integration
ab_rows = []
for nu_v in [1.0, 3.0, 10.0, 50.0]:
    A_num, _ = integrate.quad(lambda z: dz_logg(z, nu_v)**2 * g_std(z, nu_v), -np.inf, np.inf)
    B_num, _ = integrate.quad(lambda z: (1 + z*dz_logg(z, nu_v))**2 * g_std(z, nu_v), -np.inf, np.inf)
    A_cl, B_cl = metric_constants(nu_v)
    ab_rows.append((nu_v, A_num, A_cl, B_num, B_cl))


# (b) closed-form distance vs arc length along the claimed geodesic
def arclength(mu, s, nu):
    A, B = metric_constants(nu)
    dmu, ds, sm = np.diff(mu), np.diff(s), (s[:-1]+s[1:])/2
    return np.sum(np.sqrt(A*dmu**2 + B*ds**2)/sm)


dist_rows = []
for nu_v in [1.0, 3.0, 10.0, 50.0]:
    mu, s = geodesic(*p1, *p2, nu_v, n=20000)
    L_check = arclength(mu, s, nu_v)
    D_check = fr_distance(*p1, *p2, nu_v)
    dist_rows.append((nu_v, L_check, D_check, abs(L_check - D_check)))


# (c) density normalisation
I1, _ = integrate.quad(lambda x: t_density(x, *p1, 3.0), -100, 100)

ab_body = "".join(
    f"<tr><td>{nu_v:g}</td><td>{A_num:.6f}</td><td>{A_cl:.6f}</td>"
    f"<td>{B_num:.6f}</td><td>{B_cl:.6f}</td></tr>"
    for nu_v, A_num, A_cl, B_num, B_cl in ab_rows
)
dist_body = "".join(
    f"<tr><td>{nu_v:g}</td><td>{L_check:.6f}</td><td>{D_check:.6f}</td><td>{diff:.1e}</td></tr>"
    for nu_v, L_check, D_check, diff in dist_rows
)

display(HTML(f"""
<p>The direct numerical checks agree with the closed forms to numerical precision.</p>
<table>
<thead><tr><th>ν</th><th>A, numerical</th><th>A, closed form</th><th>B, numerical</th><th>B, closed form</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>{ab_body}</tbody>
</table>
<table>
<thead><tr><th>ν</th><th>geodesic arc length</th><th>closed-form distance</th><th>absolute difference</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>{dist_body}</tbody>
</table>
<p>Density normalization check over [-100,100]: {I1:.6f}.</p>
"""))
```

## What changes when $\nu$ is free

The Poincaré result is a fixed-$\nu$ statement. Let $\nu$ vary and the model becomes the three-dimensional manifold
$$
\mathcal M=\{t_\nu(\mu,\sigma):\mu\in\mathbb R,\ \sigma>0,\ \nu>0\}.
$$
Now the Fisher matrix carries a genuine shape direction. The location coordinate still decouples by symmetry, but $\sigma$ and $\nu$ no longer do, and the fixed-slice constant-curvature half-plane stops being the whole geometry.

## The full Fisher matrix

Symmetry of the standardized density keeps $\mu$ decoupled: $I_{\mu\sigma}=I_{\mu\nu}=0$. The fixed-$\nu$ block is still sitting in the upper-left corner. What's new is the signed coupling between scale and tail thickness:
$$
\boxed{\;
I(\mu,\sigma,\nu)=
\begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\nu+1}{(\nu+3)\,\sigma^2} & 0 & 0 \\[1.1em]
0 & \dfrac{2\nu}{(\nu+3)\,\sigma^2} &
-\dfrac{2}{\sigma(\nu+1)(\nu+3)} \\[1.1em]
0 & -\dfrac{2}{\sigma(\nu+1)(\nu+3)} & I_{\nu\nu}(\nu)
\end{pmatrix}
\;}
$$
$$
I_{\nu\nu}(\nu)=\tfrac14\!\left[\psi'\!\left(\tfrac{\nu}{2}\right)-\psi'\!\left(\tfrac{\nu+1}{2}\right)\right]
-\frac{\nu+5}{2\nu(\nu+1)(\nu+3)}.
$$

That trigamma term is exactly what stops the metric from staying a nice rational
form. The sign of the cross term also matters: with the usual scale coordinate
$\sigma$ we have $\partial_\sigma\log f=-(1+z\,\partial_z\log g_\nu(z))/\sigma$,
which makes the $(\sigma,\nu)$ entry negative. Both new entries are confirmed
below by direct integration of the signed score products.

```{python}
#| label: fisher3-verify
from scipy.special import digamma, polygamma
from IPython.display import HTML, display


def dnu_logg(z, nu):
    """d/dnu of log g(z;nu) at fixed z."""
    t1 = 0.5*digamma((nu+1)/2) - 0.5*digamma(nu/2) - 0.5/nu
    L  = np.log1p(z**2/nu)
    dL = (-z**2/nu**2)/(1 + z**2/nu)
    return t1 - 0.5*L - (nu+1)/2*dL


def fisher3(nu, sig=1.0):
    """Full 3x3 Fisher matrix at (mu arbitrary, sigma=sig, nu) by quadrature."""
    Smu  = lambda z: dz_logg(z, nu)          # x (-1/sig)
    Ssig = lambda z: 1 + z*dz_logg(z, nu)    # actual score is -Ssig/sig
    Snu  = lambda z: dnu_logg(z, nu)         # no 1/sig
    def E(f):
        v, _ = integrate.quad(lambda z: f(z)*g_std(z, nu), -np.inf, np.inf, limit=200)
        return v
    I = np.zeros((3, 3))
    I[0,0] = E(lambda z: Smu(z)**2)/sig**2
    I[1,1] = E(lambda z: Ssig(z)**2)/sig**2
    I[2,2] = E(lambda z: Snu(z)**2)
    I[1,2] = I[2,1] = -E(lambda z: Ssig(z)*Snu(z))/sig
    return I


def Inn_closed(nu):
    tri = polygamma(1, nu/2) - polygamma(1, (nu+1)/2)
    return 0.25*tri - (nu+5)/(2*nu*(nu+1)*(nu+3))


def Isn_closed(nu, sig=1.0):
    return -2.0/(sig*(nu+1)*(nu+3))


rows = []
for nu_v in [3.0, 10.0, 30.0]:
    I = fisher3(nu_v)
    rows.append((nu_v, I[1,2], Isn_closed(nu_v), I[2,2], Inn_closed(nu_v)))

body = "".join(
    f"<tr><td>{nu_v:g}</td><td>{num_sn:.6f}</td><td>{cl_sn:.6f}</td>"
    f"<td>{num_nn:.6f}</td><td>{cl_nn:.6f}</td></tr>"
    for nu_v, num_sn, cl_sn, num_nn, cl_nn in rows
)

display(HTML(f"""
<table>
<thead><tr><th>ν</th><th>I<sub>σν</sub>, numerical</th><th>I<sub>σν</sub>, closed form</th><th>I<sub>νν</sub>, numerical</th><th>I<sub>νν</sub>, closed form</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>{body}</tbody>
</table>
"""))
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-fisher-entries
#| fig-cap: "The two new metric components versus ν (at σ=1). $I_{\\nu\\nu}$ shown on a log scale."

nu = np.linspace(0.6, 30, 400)
Inn = 0.25*(polygamma(1, nu/2) - polygamma(1, (nu+1)/2)) - (nu+5)/(2*nu*(nu+1)*(nu+3))
Isn = -2.0/((nu+1)*(nu+3))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3.3))
ax[0].plot(nu, Inn, color=PURPLE, lw=2); ax[0].set_yscale("log")
ax[0].set_title(r"$I_{\nu\nu}(\nu)$  (trigamma term)")
ax[0].set_xlabel(r"$\nu$"); ax[0].set_ylabel(r"$I_{\nu\nu}$"); ax[0].grid(alpha=0.3)
ax[1].plot(nu, Isn, color=CORAL, lw=2)
ax[1].axhline(0, color="gray", ls=":", lw=1)
ax[1].set_title(r"signed $I_{\sigma\nu}(\nu)$ at $\sigma=1$")
ax[1].set_xlabel(r"$\nu$"); ax[1].set_ylabel(r"$I_{\sigma\nu}$"); ax[1].grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Both new entries die off as $\nu\to\infty$ ($I_{\sigma\nu}\to0$, and in fact
$I_{\nu\nu}=O(\nu^{-4})$): the shape direction decouples and the Gaussian
half-plane re-emerges as the limiting location-scale geometry.

## Numerical geodesics in the full model

Below I assemble the metric, its analytic derivatives (the $\nu$-derivative of
$I_{\nu\nu}$ drags in the tetragamma $\psi''$), and the Christoffel symbols
$\Gamma^i_{jk}=\tfrac12 g^{im}(\partial_j g_{ml}+\partial_l g_{mj}-\partial_m g_{jl})$.
Geodesics solve $\ddot\theta^{\,i}+\Gamma^i_{jk}\dot\theta^{\,j}\dot\theta^{\,k}=0$,
and to find the one between two prescribed distributions I solve the
boundary-value problem and then measure its metric arc length.

Treat what follows as a transparent numerical check rather than a production
geodesic solver. The boundary-value problem is solved directly in
$(\mu,\sigma,\nu)$, so the examples keep an eye on whether the path stays inside
the domain $\sigma>0,\nu>0$; anything more robust would work in
$(\mu,\log\sigma,\log\nu)$ or impose the domain constraints explicitly.

```{python}
#| label: geo3d-setup
#| include: false
from scipy.integrate import solve_bvp

def Inn_and_d(nu):
    """I_nunu(nu) and its derivative dI_nunu/dnu (needs tetragamma psi'')."""
    Inn = 0.25*(polygamma(1, nu/2) - polygamma(1, (nu+1)/2)) \
          - (nu+5)/(2*nu*(nu+1)*(nu+3))
    dtri = 0.25*(0.5*polygamma(2, nu/2) - 0.5*polygamma(2, (nu+1)/2))
    den  = 2*nu*(nu+1)*(nu+3)
    dden = 2*((nu+1)*(nu+3) + nu*(nu+3) + nu*(nu+1))
    dInn = dtri - (den - (nu+5)*dden)/den**2
    return Inn, dInn

def metric3(th):
    mu, sig, nu = th
    A, B = (nu+1)/(nu+3), 2*nu/(nu+3)
    Isn = -2.0/(sig*(nu+1)*(nu+3))
    Inn, _ = Inn_and_d(nu)
    return np.array([[A/sig**2, 0, 0],
                     [0, B/sig**2, Isn],
                     [0, Isn, Inn]])

def dmetric3(th):
    """Analytic dG[k] = dG/dtheta_k for k = 0:mu, 1:sigma, 2:nu."""
    mu, sig, nu = th
    A, B = (nu+1)/(nu+3), 2*nu/(nu+3)
    dA, dB = 2/(nu+3)**2, 6/(nu+3)**2
    dIsn_ds = 2.0/(sig**2*(nu+1)*(nu+3))
    dIsn_dn = 2.0*((nu+3) + (nu+1))/(sig*((nu+1)*(nu+3))**2)
    _, dInn = Inn_and_d(nu)
    dG = np.zeros((3, 3, 3))                      # k = 0 (mu): all zero
    dG[1] = [[-2*A/sig**3, 0, 0],
             [0, -2*B/sig**3, dIsn_ds],
             [0, dIsn_ds, 0]]
    dG[2] = [[dA/sig**2, 0, 0],
             [0, dB/sig**2, dIsn_dn],
             [0, dIsn_dn, dInn]]
    return dG

def christoffel(th):
    G = metric3(th); Gi = np.linalg.inv(G); dG = dmetric3(th)
    Gam = np.zeros((3, 3, 3))
    for i in range(3):
        for j in range(3):
            for l in range(3):
                Gam[i, j, l] = 0.5*sum(
                    Gi[i, m]*(dG[j][m, l] + dG[l][m, j] - dG[m][j, l])
                    for m in range(3))
    return Gam

def geo_rhs(y):
    x, v = y[:3], y[3:]
    Gam = christoffel(x)
    return np.concatenate([v, -np.einsum('ijl,j,l->i', Gam, v, v)])

def path_length3(X):
    return sum(np.sqrt((X[k+1]-X[k]) @ metric3((X[k]+X[k+1])/2) @ (X[k+1]-X[k]))
               for k in range(len(X)-1))

def geodesic3(p0, p1, n=30):
    p0, p1 = np.array(p0, float), np.array(p1, float)
    tau = np.linspace(0, 1, n)
    guess = np.outer(1-tau, p0) + np.outer(tau, p1)
    Y0 = np.vstack([guess.T, np.tile(p1-p0, (n, 1)).T])
    def rhs(t, Y):
        out = np.empty_like(Y)
        for j in range(Y.shape[1]):
            out[:, j] = geo_rhs(Y[:, j])
        return out
    def bc(ya, yb):
        return np.concatenate([ya[:3]-p0, yb[:3]-p1])
    sol = solve_bvp(rhs, bc, tau, Y0, max_nodes=6000, tol=1e-5)
    X = sol.sol(np.linspace(0, 1, 300))[:3].T
    return sol, X, path_length3(X)
```

## Leaving the fixed-$\nu$ slice

Take two distributions sharing the **same** degrees of freedom,
$P_1 = t_3(-1.2, 0.7)$ and $P_2 = t_3(1.3, 1.5)$. Pinned to the $\nu=3$ slice, the
geodesic between them has length about $1.860$. In the full three-parameter
manifold that same curve is still a legal path — it just need not be the shortest
one. With the cross-term sign handled correctly the effect turns out mild, far
milder than the earlier unsigned calculation suggested: the optimal path dips out
of the slice only a little, $\nu$ wandering between roughly $2.76$ and $3.55$, and
the length drops only slightly, to about $1.852$.

That is the honest reading. Freeing $\nu$ can shorten the path, but how far it
moves and in which direction depends on the endpoints. There is no generic plunge
toward Cauchy tails.

```{python}
#| label: bow-result
from IPython.display import HTML, display

# same-nu endpoints
p0, p1 = (-1.2, 0.7, 3.0), (1.3, 1.5, 3.0)
sol, X, L = geodesic3(p0, p1)
in_slice = fr_distance(p0[0], p0[1], p1[0], p1[1], 3.0)

# show that the fixed-nu slice is not totally geodesic
Gam0 = christoffel(np.array(p0))

nu_min, nu_max = X[:,2].min(), X[:,2].max()
display(HTML(f"""
<p>At the first endpoint,
Γ<sup>ν</sup><sub>μμ</sub> = {Gam0[2,0,0]:.3f} and
Γ<sup>ν</sup><sub>σσ</sub> = {Gam0[2,1,1]:.3f}.
These nonzero normal components show that the fixed-ν slice is not totally geodesic.</p>

<tbody>
<tr><td>full three-parameter geodesic length, L<sub>3D</sub></td><td>{L:.5f}</td></tr>
<tr><td>fixed-ν in-slice distance, d<sub>ν=3</sub></td><td>{in_slice:.5f}</td></tr>
<tr><td>ν range along the full geodesic</td><td>[{nu_min:.4f}, {nu_max:.4f}]</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
"""))
```

When the two endpoints sit in the same fixed-$\nu$ slice, the fixed-$\nu$ distance
is a constrained distance, and so it can only be an **upper bound** on the true
three-parameter Fisher--Rao distance. Here the bound is tight: freeing $\nu$ buys
a small shortcut, not a dramatic heavy-tail detour. The two distances coincide
only when $\nu$ is genuinely pinned down as a modelling constraint.

## Fixed $\nu$ versus free $\nu$

| Quantity | Fixed $\nu$ | Free $\nu$ |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Manifold dimension | $2$ | $3$ |
| Curvature | constant $-(\nu+3)/(2\nu)$ on each fixed slice | not captured by one fixed-slice constant-curvature model |
| Metric form | rational in $\nu$ | trigamma $\psi'$ in $I_{\nu\nu}$ |
| Geodesics | half-ellipses (closed form) | numerical (BVP) |
| Distance | closed form (§6) | numerical; §6 is an upper bound when endpoints lie in one fixed-$\nu$ slice |
| Same-$\nu$ shortest path | constrained to stay in slice | may leave the slice; in the example only mildly |
